clue.text: Bombers essentially level city bordering lake without shame

indicators.note: What is essential to a word is its very centre, so only the letter at its heart is kept.
A thing that borders another runs along each side of it.

blocks.note: BOMBERS has seven letters and the middle one is B
to raze a building is to level it to the ground
NY is New York, the city that goes by its two letters
l = lake, as printed on maps

explanation.surface: Bombers flattening a city on a lakeshore, with no apparent conscience about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the trap: it reads as an instruction to take something away, and it is half the definition. 'Essentially' is the one to learn — the essence of a word is the letter at its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To act brazenly is to act openly and without a flicker of shame, which is the adverb the definition spells out.

clue.text: Bachelor with no date gatecrashing weirdly arcane shindig

indicators.note: Something done weirdly is done out of its usual shape, and letters out of their usual shape are letters in a new order.
A gatecrasher gets inside a party he was never asked to, so these letters push in among the others.

blocks.note: b = bachelor, the degree's abbreviation in BA and BSc
anagram fodder, six letters, which end up either side of the gatecrashers
n.d. is the bibliographer's mark for a book that gives no date of publication

explanation.surface: An unattached bachelor turning up uninvited at a strange old-fashioned party.
explanation.walkthrough: The bachelor is B, the letter after a degree, and his lack of a partner is n.d., the two letters a cataloguer writes on a book with no date. A barn dance has a caller shouting the steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindig is a noisy, boisterous party, and a barn dance — fiddles, a caller, everyone swinging their partner — is exactly that kind of evening.

clue.text: Genuine gold article conservationists originally insured comprehensively

indicators.note: Where a word originates is its opening letter, so only the first letter of each word that follows is taken.

blocks.note: Au is gold's symbol in the periodic table, from Latin aurum
'the' is the definite article
the National Trust is the British charity that looks after historic houses and coastline
the first letters of INSURED and COMPREHENSIVELY

explanation.surface: A gold object that the heritage people insured in full from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: Three of the four pieces are conventions rather than synonyms: Au off the periodic table, THE as 'article', and NT for the National Trust, whose initials appear on half the stately homes in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Something authentic is the real article rather than a copy or a fake, which is what calling it genuine says.

clue.text: Bail out of plane circling around south of Spain

indicators.note: Something circling another goes right round it.
In a down entry south means further down the column.

blocks.note: E is Spain's international vehicle plate, from España
a jet is a plane, and it opens up to take the next letter
c = circa, the 'around' written in front of an uncertain date

explanation.surface: A pilot baling out of an aircraft circling somewhere off southern Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words side by side look like the same instruction: 'circling' is the container, while 'around' is only the letter C, from circa. Spain is E, the oval sticker on a Spanish car.
explanation.definitionFit: To eject is to be fired clear of an aircraft in the seat, which is what a pilot means by bailing out.

clue.text: Strip naked in backstreet toilet

indicators.note: Stripped of its clothes a word loses its outermost letters and only what they covered is left.
'In' puts what came before it inside what comes after.

blocks.note: a lane is a narrow back street
STRIP with its outer letters taken off keeps only TRI

explanation.surface: Someone taking all their clothes off in a back alley.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Strip' as the instruction; it is the word being undressed, and 'naked' is what does the undressing. A latrine is the trench or hut a camp digs for the purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: A latrine is a communal toilet in a barracks or a camp, dug or built rather than plumbed.

clue.text: Turn back women wearing jeans

indicators.note: Turned back, a run of letters faces the other way and is read from its far end.
Clothes go round the person in them.

blocks.note: Levi's are the jeans, and they close round the next letter
w = women, as on a lavatory door

explanation.surface: Women in jeans being turned away at a door.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface keeps you among the denim, and the brand is the piece wanted: Levi Strauss's jeans are the crossword's standard pair. The whole assembly is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To swivel is to turn on the spot about a fixed point, the way a chair or a pair of hips does.

clue.text: Court finally seized stately home's fuel reserves

indicators.note: What comes finally in a word is the letter that finishes it, and that letter is all this takes.

blocks.note: to court somebody is to woo them
the last letter of SEIZED
a great British house is a pile — a stately pile — and the 's of the surface is the letter that makes it plural

explanation.surface: A court at last confiscating the logs stored at a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' looks like the courtroom the rest of the sentence is about, and it is the verb, to woo. A pile is what the British call a grand house, which is where the logs are stacked.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodpile is the stack of logs a house keeps for its fires, so several of them are reserves of fuel.

clue.text: Regulating device found in retrieval vehicle

indicators.note: What is found in something is already sitting there, so the answer is written out in the words themselves.

blocks.note: the letters sit in the words as written, starting at the seventh letter of the first and running across the space into the second

explanation.surface: A component turning up inside a recovery truck.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers are laid across a word break on purpose, because the eye stops at spaces; this one starts three letters before the end of the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A valve opens and shuts to control what passes through a pipe, which is regulation by machinery.

clue.text: Record in auditorium for composer

indicators.note: An auditorium is where things are heard, so what counts is how the word sounds rather than how it is spelt.

blocks.note: to record items one after another is to list them, and the Hungarian's name comes out of the mouth the same way

explanation.surface: Noting something down in a concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like a recording being made in the hall and means the humblest kind of writing down. Franz Liszt was the piano virtuoso of the 1840s whose recitals left audiences swooning.
explanation.definitionFit: Liszt wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies and the B minor sonata, so composer is the plain job title for him.

clue.text: European doctors on hand for periods of withdrawal

indicators.note: In an across entry what is written on something else has been laid over it from the left, so the piece after 'on' is entered first.

blocks.note: a hand is a right or a left, and r is the short form of right
e = European
a doctor treats patients, so the verb doctors is treats

explanation.surface: European medics standing by to help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' reads as a plural noun and works as a verb. 'On' is the piece of grammar to learn: in an across clue it lays one thing over another from the left, so what follows it goes in first.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreat is a spell spent withdrawn from the world, whether a religious one or an army's pull-back, so several are periods of withdrawal.

clue.text: Tree-huggers fine revolutionary, unfortunately

indicators.note: A revolution takes a thing full circle, so the letters in front of it are read the other way round.

blocks.note: fine = OK, and it turns round
alas = unfortunately

explanation.surface: Green campaigners regrettably rather taken with a revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tree-huggers' is the joke: the mocking word for environmental protesters, handed to the animals that actually spend their lives clamped to a trunk. OK reversed is the crossword's usual source of KO.
explanation.definitionFit: A koala grips a eucalyptus all day and eats little else, so the insult aimed at environmentalists lands on the creature doing it literally.

clue.text: Intelligence gatherer dismisses posh British national

indicators.note: To dismiss something is to send it away, so the letter named next leaves the word.

blocks.note: a scout is sent ahead to find out what is there
U is the label for upper-class usage, from the U and non-U talk of the 1950s; the letter is the one dropped

explanation.surface: A spy writing off a well-bred Briton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intelligence gatherer' points at spies, and the one wanted is the soldier sent ahead to look. U for posh comes from the U and non-U lists of upper-class words that amused Britain in the fifties.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scot is somebody from Scotland, and Scotland is part of Britain, which makes one a British national.

clue.text: Lived with the Spanish in outskirts of Detroit

indicators.note: 'In' drops what came before it inside what comes after.
The outskirts of a place are its edges, so only the first and last letters of the word are kept.

blocks.note: DETROIT keeps only its edges, D and T
w/ is the standard short form of with
'the' in Spanish is el

explanation.surface: Someone who lived on the edge of Detroit with Spaniards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish' never means people from Spain in a cryptic — it asks for their word for 'the', the same loan that supplies LE and LA from French. W for with comes from the w/ of scribbled notes.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to live there, and the past tense dwelt answers 'lived' exactly.

clue.text: Just starting remarkably nice pint after one

indicators.note: Something remarkable is out of the ordinary, and letters out of their ordinary order make an anagram.
'After' says which side of the other piece these letters land on: they follow it.

blocks.note: i = one, the Roman numeral
anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A remarkably good pint ordered after the first one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just starting' is the definition rather than a note on the evening: incipient means barely under way, a cold or a rebellion in its first stage. The Roman I for 'one' is the commonest single letter in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incipient has only just begun to exist, which is what 'just starting' describes.

clue.text: Important reason for refusing service in restaurant?

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the second definition asks for a noun phrase; the licence, flagged by the question mark, is that the letters re-split as NO TABLE.

definitions.text: reason for refusing service in restaurant

blocks.note: the everyday sense, worth taking note of

blocks.clueFragment: reason for refusing service in restaurant?
blocks.note: move the gap two letters along and this is what the head waiter says when the room is full

explanation.surface: Why a restaurant might turn a hungry diner away at the door.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is shuffled, hidden or reversed here; the entire trick is where the space falls between the letters. A fully booked restaurant has no table, and the question mark owns up to how playful that reading is.
explanation.definitionFit: Notable means worth remarking on; read as two words it is the excuse a full restaurant gives, no table.

clue.text: Beating GOP rebel with a big stick!

indicators.note: To beat a mixture is to knock it about until nothing is where it started, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; the GOP is the Grand Old Party, the American Republicans
the single letter joins the fodder

explanation.surface: A Republican dissident being thrashed with a big stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beating' opens the clue where a definition usually sits, which is what makes the anagram hard to spot. The answer's home is the British brush-off: wouldn't touch it with a bargepole.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargepole is the long pole used to shove a canal barge off the bank, a big stick in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Anecdotes about extremely nondescript gifts

indicators.note: Something written about another wraps round the outside of it.
The extremes of a word are its two ends, so its first and last letters are all that come out.

blocks.note: tales = anecdotes, and they open up to take the next pair
the outer letters of NONDESCRIPT

explanation.surface: Stories being told about somebody utterly unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gifts' is not parcels but the things you were born able to do — the parable of the talents, where the money handed out stands for exactly that, is why the word carries both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A talent is a natural gift, an ability given rather than earned, which is the sense the biblical parable left in English.

clue.text: Telling state to protect a reporter on vacation

indicators.note: To protect something is to close round it and keep it inside.
A word on vacation has moved out and left the middle empty, so only the letters at each end stay behind.

blocks.note: a nation is a state, and it opens up to take the rest
the word itself, one letter
REPORTER empties out, leaving the R at each end

explanation.surface: A country looking after a journalist who is away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telling' looks like the adjective in 'a telling remark' and is the noun, the act of telling a story. 'On vacation' is the setter saying a word has been vacated, emptied of all but its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A narration is the telling of a story aloud, so the two nouns name the same act.

clue.text: Aboard ship, decorator without a harnessing line shivers

indicators.note: 'Without' is the older sense here, lacking, so the letter named next is dropped.
To harness something is to strap it in, so this letter is buckled inside the word before it.

blocks.note: SS is a steamship, and the rest goes between the two letters
painter and decorator is one trade in Britain
the A comes out of PAINTER, leaving PINTER
l = line, the letter strapped inside

explanation.surface: A decorator on board a ship, shaking with cold now his safety line has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shivers' is the sailor's noun, not the shaking: the splinters a wooden hull breaks into, as in shiver my timbers. Britain hires a painter and decorator as one man, which is where PAINTER comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A shiver is a splinter of wood, the sense preserved in 'shiver my timbers' — a hull smashing into fragments.

clue.text: Passage emerging from former church run by discontented priest

indicators.note: A word robbed of its contents keeps only the letters on the outside.

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, and ex- means former
CE is the Church of England, the established church
r = run on a cricket scorecard
PRIEST loses its contents and keeps P and T

explanation.surface: A corridor leading out of a deconsecrated church that a grumpy priest runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' is the pun worth catching: the priest is not sulking, he has had his contents removed. R for run comes off a cricket scorecard and turns up in a hundred clues.
explanation.definitionFit: An excerpt is a passage lifted out of a longer text, the quoted piece rather than the corridor.

clue.text: Mistake blood group in report

indicators.note: Something reported is spoken, so the words are to be heard rather than read.

blocks.note: the blood groups are A, B, AB and O, and type O said aloud is the answer

explanation.surface: A patient's blood group written down wrongly in a medical report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' is the giveaway, asking to be heard, though the surface wants you picturing a document on a desk. The four blood groups are A, B, AB and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A typo is a slip of the finger at a keyboard, the commonest small mistake in anything printed.

clue.text: Some surreal art simply reflected atmospheric phenomenon

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows, a run of letters taken straight out of the words as written.
A reflection comes back the other way round, so the run is read from its end.

blocks.note: surreaL ART SIMply holds LARTSIM, which turns round into the answer

explanation.surface: A piece of surrealist art shown plainly in a mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: The mistral is the cold north wind that funnels down the Rhône valley to the French Mediterranean for days on end, blamed there for bad tempers. Any clue mentioning mirrors is worth scanning backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The mistral is a named wind of southern France, dry and violent, which makes it a phenomenon of the atmosphere.

clue.text: Musical ornament mentor modified to conceal diamonds

indicators.note: Something modified is no longer as it was, and letters no longer as they were are letters rearranged.
To conceal a thing is to keep it out of sight inside, so this letter goes within the others.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
d = diamonds, one of the four card suits

explanation.surface: A mentor altered so as to hide the diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: A mordent is the quick flick down to the next note and back that a player makes when a small zigzag appears over the stave. D for diamonds comes from the bridge table, where every suit has its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A mordent is one of the standard written ornaments of music, a rapid alternation with the note next door.

clue.text: Daughter initially implied suspicious character is dog killer?

indicators.note: A word's initial is the letter it begins with, and that is all each of these words gives up.

blocks.note: d = daughter, the abbreviation on a family tree
the first letters of IMPLIED and SUSPICIOUS
a person's temper is their character or disposition

explanation.surface: A daughter hinting from the outset that some shady type has been killing dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' is the disposition sense rather than a person in a story — your temper is the character you were given. Distemper is also the chalky wall paint decorators mixed before emulsion arrived.
explanation.definitionFit: Canine distemper is the viral disease that kills unvaccinated dogs, so the question mark's rough label points at the illness.

clue.text: Given the chop, investigators turned on journalist

indicators.note: Turned round, a word is read from its last letter back to its first.
In a down entry one thing sits on another by resting above it, so the detectives are written in at the top.

blocks.note: the CID is Britain's Criminal Investigation Department, its plain-clothes detectives
ed = editor

explanation.surface: Detectives rounding on a newspaperman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' does two jobs at once: it reads as detectives rounding on somebody, and it tells you those three letters go in backwards. The CID is the branch a British detective belongs to.
explanation.definitionFit: Diced food has been chopped into small cubes, so it has literally been given the chop — the phrase the surface uses for being sacked.

clue.text: Posed entertaining question, in short

indicators.note: To entertain a guest is to have them inside the house, so these letters are taken in.

blocks.note: somebody who posed for a portrait sat for it
qu. is the standard short form of question

explanation.surface: Somebody sitting there taking a question in good part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' does two jobs: it shortens question to qu., and its last word is the definition. Squat means low and thick-set for its width rather than merely small.
explanation.definitionFit: A squat building or figure is short and broad, so the adjective answers 'short' directly.

clue.text: Emptied bin filled with uncooked meat

indicators.note: A word emptied has lost everything between its ends, so its first and last letters are what remain.
What a thing is filled with goes inside it.

blocks.note: BIN loses its middle and keeps B and N
uncooked = raw

explanation.surface: A bin tipped out and packed with raw meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Brawn is the British cold cut made from a boiled pig's head set in its own jelly and sold sliced at the butcher's — the same word as the one meaning muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: Brawn is potted meat from a pig's head, so 'meat' is the plain label for it.

clue.text: Spew black lies, oddly about Switzerland

indicators.note: Taken oddly, a word yields only the letters in its odd positions, the first, the third and so on.
Turned about, a pair of letters faces the other way.

blocks.note: B = black, as stamped on a pencil
the first and third letters of LIES
CH is Switzerland's international code, from its Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica

explanation.surface: Spouting black lies about the Swiss every now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container instruction and is not — it turns two letters round. CH is on every Swiss numberplate: the Latin name is used because the country has four languages and no favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To belch is to bring wind up noisily, and a chimney or a volcano belches out what it spews.

clue.text: Ticket scam captivates press

indicators.note: To captivate is to take captive, so what follows is held inside.

blocks.note: a con is a scam, and it closes round the next three letters
OUP is Oxford University Press, a press in the publishing sense

explanation.surface: A ticket fraud that has the newspapers spellbound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' is the publisher, not the newspapers the surface suggests: OUP is Oxford University Press, and CUP its Cambridge rival, both regulars in clues like this.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupon is the printed slip you tear off and hand over, which makes it a ticket for a discount or an entry.

clue.text: Decreased rent, to Spooner's eternal torment

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to trade the opening sounds of two words, so that trade has to be undone here.

blocks.note: a rent that decreased fell, and rent is also hire; swap the front sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: A cut in the rent, announced by the Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooner clues want the innocent pair found first, so look for two plain words before attempting any swap. William Spooner was the Oxford warden whose tangled announcements made the trick famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellfire is the everlasting burning promised to the damned, which is torment with no end to it.

clue.text: Doubt misers regularly admitted responsibilities

indicators.note: Letting letters through at regular intervals means taking every other one, beginning with the first.

blocks.note: the first letter of DOUBT MISERS and every other one after it, the count running straight across the space

explanation.surface: Misers owning up now and then to what they owe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitted' looks like an instruction to put something inside, and it is letting letters through instead. A run of alternate letters spanning two words is the harder version of the device, because the count ignores the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Your duties are the things you are answerable for doing, which is what responsibilities are.

clue.text: Fellow leaving attractive soprano inscriptions

indicators.note: Somebody leaving walks out, and so does the letter that stands for him.

blocks.note: f = fellow, the F of a learned society's letters
fetching = attractive, and it is the word the F walks out of
s = soprano on a choral score

explanation.surface: A man walking out on a good-looking singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow leaving' reads as a chap making his exit and means a single letter doing so. The old seducer's line about coming up to see my etchings is what the surface is flirting with.
explanation.definitionFit: An etching is a design bitten into a metal plate with acid, so the marks cut into the surface are inscriptions.
